passage:
Dear Baljeet,
Sorry for not replying for three weeks. Honestly, Bengaluru has been harder than I told everyone. I have a room, classes, a canteen card. Everything works. But I don't know anyone. Some days I can't even make myself do the laundry. Last Sunday I sat looking at my assignment for two hours and typed four lines. Silly, na? Back home I could do ten assignments with you shouting cricket scores at me.
Something small changed on Thursday, though. Two boys from my floor, one from Assam and one from Kerala, knocked to ask if I wanted to split a pizza. We ended up talking till 1 a.m. Since then we've done our assignments together in the common room. I finished two this week. 🙂
Missing home a bit less,
Lokesh

qa.q: What did the two boys from Lokesh's floor ask?
qa.a: They knocked to ask if Lokesh wanted to split a pizza.

qa.q: Why could Lokesh barely manage laundry or an assignment in the first weeks?
qa.a: With no one to talk to, even easy tasks felt heavy; loneliness drained Lokesh's energy more than the work itself.

qa.q: What choice after Thursday helped Lokesh's motivation?
qa.a: Lokesh started doing assignments with the two new friends in the common room, and that small circle made finishing work feel possible again.

qa.q: How might Baljeet feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Baljeet may feel sad about how lonely Lokesh had been, but relieved to read about the new friends and the two finished assignments.

grounding: In a letter, a student in a new city describes easy tasks feeling hard until a small circle of friends forms.

passage: People think moving to Delhi for my master's was exciting. I'm Rukmini, and for the first two months I barely survived. I'd come back from class and lie on my bed at the paying-guest house with my shoes on. Buying groceries felt like climbing a hill. Answering my mother's calls took energy I didn't have. I kept telling myself, "It's only laundry, just do it," and still didn't. Then one day in the library, a girl named Aparna asked if I was also stuck on the statistics assignment. We worked on it together. The next week she brought two friends. Now there are four of us, we cook instant noodles on Sundays, and I'm near the top of the stats class. It wasn't the city that changed. It was having three people.

qa.q: Where did Rukmini meet Aparna?
qa.a: In the library, when Aparna asked if Rukmini was also stuck on the statistics assignment.

qa.q: Why did buying groceries feel like climbing a hill for Rukmini?
qa.a: Alone in a new city with no one to connect with, Rukmini had little energy, so even small tasks felt huge.

qa.q: What turning point shows the effect of a small circle?
qa.a: Working on statistics with Aparna, then as a group of four, gave Rukmini company and a reason to keep going, and the stats marks climbed.

qa.q: What might Rukmini's mother notice on the phone calls now?
qa.a: She may hear more energy and stories about friends and Sunday cooking, instead of the tired voice she had worried about.

grounding: A student in a new city struggles with simple tasks until a small group of friends forms and motivation returns.

passage: Nitin here. My roommate Varun moved to Mumbai from a small town near Jhansi for engineering. For his first month I barely saw him eat properly. He'd sit at his desk with the lab manual open for hours, turning the same page. He missed two submissions, which surprised me, because he's clearly smart. He hardly spoke. I can't say I knew what was going on inside him. Then the hostel held a Bundelkhand food evening, and three seniors from his district found him. They started meeting every Friday for chai at the gate. Within two weeks Varun had caught up on both submissions and joined the robotics club. Last night he laughed at something on his phone, loudly. It was the first time I'd heard it.

qa.q: What did three seniors from Varun's district start doing?
qa.a: They started meeting every Friday for chai at the gate.

qa.q: Why might Varun have turned the same page for hours?
qa.a: Far from home and with no one to talk to, he may have felt too lonely and low to concentrate, even on work he could do.

qa.q: What could Nitin have done earlier, knowing what helped?
qa.a: Nitin could have invited Varun to eat together or to a club meeting, offering even a tiny circle before the seniors found him.

qa.q: How does Nitin experience the change in Varun?
qa.a: Nitin, who was puzzled by the missed submissions, is struck by hearing Varun laugh loudly for the first time.

grounding: A roommate watches a lonely student struggle with easy work until a small circle from home forms and his effort returns.

passage:
First week of August: Karthik had moved from Tirunelveli to Kolkata for his master's. Everything was hard in a stupid way. He couldn't make himself go to the post office to change his address. He ate biscuits for dinner three nights running rather than ask the mess what was vegetarian. Lectures went in one ear and out.
Late August: In the lab, Sabina from Kerala asked him to hold a burette and noticed his accent. 'Tamil? Come for dinner on Friday. A few of us cook together.' He almost said no.
September: Five of them now, cooking every Friday in the hostel kitchen, arguing about how much tamarind is too much. Karthik finished two assignments early, changed his address, and even asked a question in class. Same city, same course. Just five people who knew his name.

qa.q: What did Karthik eat for dinner three nights running?
qa.a: Biscuits.

qa.q: Why did simple tasks like the post office feel so hard to Karthik in August?
qa.a: Alone in a strange city with nobody who knew him, Karthik had little energy to push; the lack of connection drained his motivation even for small things.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what did it change?
qa.a: Accepting Sabina's Friday dinner invitation, though he almost said no; with one small circle, Karthik finished assignments early, sorted his address and spoke up in class.

qa.q: How might Sabina see that invitation looking back?
qa.a: Sabina may have seen it as a small friendly gesture to someone from the south, without knowing how much it changed Karthik's whole semester.

grounding: A student alone in a new city finds even easy tasks hard, and his motivation returns once one small circle of friends forms.

passage:
Irawati, you'll be in Chennai next month, and you're scared of being lonely. Good that you said it. Let me tell you about my first year in Hyderabad.
I was nineteen, from a village near Aligarh. Nobody in college knew me. I'd sit in the library with a book open for hours and read the same page. I stopped washing my clothes on time. I even stopped calling Ammi, because I had nothing good to tell her.
Then one Sunday a senior from the next room, Venkat, knocked. 'Asif, you play carrom?' I didn't, really. He taught me. Soon there were four of us every Sunday, fighting over the red queen.
That year my marks went up by twenty percent. Nothing else changed. Just four boys and a carrom board.
Find your carrom board, beta.

qa.q: What game did Venkat invite young Asif to play?
qa.a: Carrom.

qa.q: Why did young Asif stop calling Ammi?
qa.a: He was lonely and struggling, with 'nothing good to tell her'; the lack of connection made him feel he had failed.

qa.q: What choice changed young Asif's year, and why?
qa.a: Saying yes to Venkat's carrom invitation, though he didn't really play; that small circle of four gave him connection, and his marks rose.

qa.q: How might Irawati feel hearing this before leaving for Chennai?
qa.a: Irawati may feel relieved that loneliness is common and can ease, and more hopeful about finding one small circle in Chennai.

grounding: An elder recalls being lonely and unmotivated as a student in a new city until one small circle formed around a carrom board.

passage:
Week two. Mohit had been in Bengaluru for fourteen days and hadn't spoken to anyone beyond 'one tea'. Even small things felt heavy: the laundry bag sat in the corner for a week, and he missed a morning lecture because he couldn't make himself get up. His mother asked on the phone if he was eating. He said yes.
Week four. In the chemistry lab, Himani, who sat next to him, asked if he wanted to join three of them studying in the library on Thursdays. He almost said no. He said okay.
Week six. Thursdays had become the fixed point of Mohit's week. He did his laundry on Wednesdays so he'd have a clean shirt. He finished the problem sets early so he'd have questions for the group. On Sunday he called his mother and talked for forty minutes, mostly about Himani's terrible jokes.

qa.q: When did the group study in the library?
qa.a: They studied in the library on Thursdays.

qa.q: Why did even small tasks feel heavy to Mohit in week two?
qa.a: He felt lonely and disconnected in a new city, and without anyone around, his energy and motivation drained.

qa.q: What helped Mohit's motivation return?
qa.a: Saying yes to Himani's small study group gave him a fixed, connected point in the week that he wanted to prepare for.

qa.q: How might Mohit's mother feel on the Sunday call?
qa.a: She would likely feel relieved and happy hearing him talk for forty minutes about new friends.

grounding: Over six weeks, a student alone in a new city struggles with even easy tasks until a small study circle forms and his motivation returns.

passage: Binita, you say you can't even make yourself go to the canteen in Delhi. Your Pooja Mausi knows that feeling well. When I was nineteen, I came to Mumbai for my B.Com and stayed in a working women's hostel near Dadar. For two months I spoke to nobody. I stopped washing my clothes properly. I'd sit with my textbook for hours and read the same page. I told my mother on the phone I was busy. Then one evening the girl in the next room, a nurse from Kerala called Susan, knocked and asked if I'd share her fish curry because she'd made too much. Then another girl joined us, then a third. Every Sunday, we cooked together. Within a month I was doing well in my class tests. The work was the same. I just wasn't alone anymore. So tell me, is there anyone on your floor who cooks?

qa.q: Where did Pooja stay in Mumbai?
qa.a: She stayed in a working women's hostel near Dadar.

qa.q: Why did Pooja read the same page for hours?
qa.a: She felt lonely and cut off, speaking to nobody for two months, and that isolation made even easy tasks feel hard.

qa.q: What turning point in the story brought Pooja's motivation back?
qa.a: Susan inviting her to share fish curry, which grew into a small Sunday cooking circle.

qa.q: How might Susan have seen the quiet girl next door?
qa.a: Susan may have sensed she was lonely and offered food as a simple, kind way to connect.

grounding: An aunt recalls how loneliness in a new city made easy tasks hard, and how one small circle of friends brought her energy back.

passage: Payal's first monsoon in Kolkata came with a week of waterlogged streets, and her college shut its gates. She sat alone in her rented room in Behala, far from Nagpur, with rain drumming on the tin roof. An assignment that should have taken an hour took three days. She ate biscuits for dinner because walking to the kitchen felt like too much. On the fourth evening the power went out, and someone knocked. It was Sabina from the room upstairs, holding a candle and a pack of cards. 'Everyone's in the landlady's hall. Come.' Payal nearly said no. Instead she went down. Four girls, a candle, a game of rummy, and hot khichuri from the landlady. They laughed about the rain. The next morning Payal finished her next assignment in an hour, and texted Sabina: 'Same time tonight?'

qa.q: What did the landlady serve?
qa.a: She served hot khichuri.

qa.q: Why did a one-hour assignment take Payal three days?
qa.a: She felt lonely and cut off in a new city during the floods, and without connection her motivation drained.

qa.q: What helped Payal's energy return?
qa.a: Saying yes to Sabina's invitation and joining the small group in the landlady's hall gave her connection, and her next assignment took an hour.

qa.q: How might Sabina feel getting 'Same time tonight?'
qa.a: Sabina would likely feel pleased that her invitation helped and that a friendship was forming.

grounding: During a flooded week in a new city, a lonely student struggles with easy tasks until a small circle forms and her motivation returns.

passage:
Ojas had been in Bengaluru for three weeks. He had not spoken more than ten sentences to anyone.
Simple things felt enormous. Doing laundry meant finding the machine, finding coins, finding the courage to ask someone how it worked. He wore the same two T-shirts. He skipped the canteen because eating alone felt so obvious. His assignments sat unopened.
One evening, a boy from the next room knocked. “I'm Vikas. We're making instant noodles in the corridor. You want some?”
Ojas almost said no. He said yes.
There were four of them, sitting on the floor, arguing about cricket. Someone showed him the laundry trick.
The next morning, Ojas opened his first assignment. It wasn't easier. But it felt possible.

qa.q: How long had Ojas been in Bengaluru?
qa.a: He had been there for three weeks.

qa.q: Why did simple tasks feel enormous to Ojas?
qa.a: He felt lonely and disconnected, so even asking about laundry or eating alone felt overwhelming.

qa.q: What helped Ojas start his assignments again?
qa.a: Saying yes to Vikas's invitation and finding a small circle, which made the hard tasks feel possible.

qa.q: How might Vikas see the new boy in the next room?
qa.a: Vikas probably noticed Ojas seemed alone and felt kind enough to invite him in.

grounding: The passage shows a student in a strange city struggling with easy tasks through loneliness, and his motivation improving when a small circle forms.

passage:
“Is this seat free?”
“Yes. Sit.” Avni moved her tray. “You're new, right? Mass Comm?”
“Vijay. Yes. From Jorhat.”
“Avni. From Bhopal. Also new.”
“You don't look new.”
“I'm faking it. I cried in the bathroom on Monday.”
Vijay laughed, surprised. “I haven't submitted a single assignment. I sit in my room and watch the ceiling fan.”
“Same. I took forty minutes to buy a bus pass because I didn't want to ask anyone where the counter was.”
“Forty minutes!”
“It's a big counter.”
They both laughed.
“Want to do the media ethics reading together?” Avni asked. “My room's too quiet.”
“Library at five?”
“Five.”
Vijay walked out of the canteen and realised he was humming. He did the reading that evening. It took an hour. The week before, it had taken three days to not start it.

qa.q: How long did Avni take to buy a bus pass?
qa.a: She took forty minutes to buy a bus pass.

qa.q: Why had Vijay not submitted any assignments?
qa.a: He felt lonely and stuck in his room, and without connection even easy tasks felt impossible to start.

qa.q: What small step helped them both?
qa.a: Agreeing to do the reading together at the library at five, which created a tiny circle and made starting easier.

qa.q: How does Avni experience meeting Vijay?
qa.a: Avni seems relieved and warm, glad to find someone else who is also struggling and new.

grounding: The dialogue shows two students lonely in a new city, and motivation returning once a small circle forms.

passage:
My first month in Pune, I couldn't do anything. I'm Sudha, and at home in Nellore I'd been the organised one. Here I lay on my hostel bed and couldn't even make myself walk to the photocopy shop. The lecture notes piled up.
It wasn't that the work was hard. It was that nobody knew my name. Every task felt like climbing a hill with no one at the top.
Then Nikita, a girl from my practical batch, asked if I'd join a Sunday cooking group, four of us sharing one tiny stove in her PG. We made terrible upma and laughed.
After that, things shifted. On Monday I went to the photocopy shop. On Tuesday I finished two pending labs. The work hadn't changed. I just had four people who'd ask me how it went.

qa.q: What did the Sunday cooking group make?
qa.a: They made terrible upma on one tiny stove in Nikita's PG.

qa.q: Why couldn't Sudha walk to the photocopy shop in the first month?
qa.a: Sudha felt lonely and invisible, since nobody knew Sudha's name, so every task felt like climbing a hill alone.

qa.q: What helped Sudha's motivation return?
qa.a: Joining a small circle through the cooking group, which gave Sudha people who cared how things went.

qa.q: How might Nikita see the invitation she made?
qa.a: Nikita probably thought of it as a small, friendly gesture, without knowing how much it helped.

grounding: The reflection shows a student in a new city unable to face easy tasks through loneliness, until a small circle forms.

passage:
Hostel warden's note, first-year, by Keerthana
Tarun came from Guwahati to Chennai in July. He's bright, but he's struggling with small things: he hasn't opened a bank account, missed two forms, eats alone at odd hours. Today he said, "Even buying a SIM card feels too hard. I don't know anyone. Nothing feels worth doing." He's not failing anything yet, but everything has become heavy.
I don't think he lacks ability. He lacks a single friend here.
What I did next: I introduced him to three first-years from the northeast who meet on Sunday evenings to cook together, and to Arvind from his department, who also plays football. I'll check how he's doing next week.
Update, Friday: Tarun went to the Sunday dinner and played football twice. He opened his bank account on Thursday, with Arvind, and says the forms feel easier now.

qa.q: Where did Tarun come from?
qa.a: He came from Guwahati to Chennai in July.

qa.q: Why were even easy tasks hard for Tarun?
qa.a: Tarun felt lonely and disconnected in a strange city, so everything felt heavy and not worth doing.

qa.q: What did Keerthana do that helped Tarun's motivation return?
qa.a: Keerthana introduced him to students who cook together on Sundays and to Arvind who plays football, giving him a small circle.

qa.q: How might Arvind see Tarun after going to the bank together?
qa.a: Arvind probably sees a new friend, not just a classmate who needed help.

grounding: A warden notes a student in a new city struggling with easy tasks for lack of connection, and motivation returning once a small circle forms.

passage:
Wednesday
Two months in Bengaluru now. I thought college would feel exciting. Instead, I can't even make myself go to the stationery shop across the road. I haven't unpacked my second suitcase. I eat biscuits for dinner because the mess feels so loud and I don't know anyone.
Tonight my neighbour on the floor, Rafiq, knocked. He's from Hyderabad. "Some of us from the first year are doing a study circle on Thursday nights. Kannada tea and complaints about calculus. Want to come?" I nearly said no. Then I said yes.
Even just saying yes made me feel lighter. I unpacked the second suitcase tonight. I bought a new pen from the stationery shop at nine pm, just because I suddenly felt like I could.
Thursday. Study circle. I'm actually looking forward to something.
Manjula

qa.q: Which suitcase had Manjula not unpacked?
qa.a: The second suitcase.

qa.q: Why couldn't Manjula make it across the road to the stationery shop?
qa.a: Manjula felt lonely and disconnected in the new city, so even easy tasks felt too hard.

qa.q: Why did saying yes to Rafiq change things so quickly?
qa.a: It promised a small circle, and even that hint of connection gave Manjula the energy to unpack and go out.

qa.q: How might Rafiq feel if he knew his invitation helped so much?
qa.a: Rafiq would probably feel glad and a little surprised that a simple knock made such a difference.

grounding: A student in a new city finds even easy tasks hard for lack of connection, and motivation returns as soon as a small circle forms.

passage:
The winter Vikas moved to Tezpur for his diploma, fog sat on the river till noon, and he found himself unable to do the simplest things. Buying a SIM card took three trips because he couldn't make himself ask the shopkeeper to repeat. He ate the same egg roll every night because the canteen queue was full of people who knew each other. He had two assignments open and started neither.
In the third week, the boy from the next room, Varun, knocked. "We're cooking khichdi on the heater. Three of us. Want to come?"
Vikas almost said no. He went. They talked till midnight about home, cricket, the terrible fog.
After that there was someone to ask about the physics lab and someone to walk to class with. By the end of the month he had submitted both assignments.

qa.q: What did Varun invite Vikas to?
qa.a: Khichdi cooked on the heater, with three of them.

qa.q: Why did simple tasks feel so hard for Vikas at first?
qa.a: Vikas felt lonely and awkward in a town where everyone seemed to know each other, and that isolation drained his energy even for easy things.

qa.q: What helped Vikas, and what could other new students take from it?
qa.a: Saying yes to one small invitation built a circle to ask and walk with; a new student can accept, or make, a small offer like shared food even when feeling shy.

qa.q: How might Varun see the evening?
qa.a: Varun probably saw a quiet neighbour eating alone and wanted to include him; for Varun it may have been just khichdi, but for Vikas it was a turning point.

grounding: A student alone in a new town struggles even with easy tasks until one small circle of friends forms.
